campaignsText: ZeffSec’s operational tempo is characterized by episodic bursts of high‑profile attacks, most notably the March 2026 ArvanCloud DDoS that leveraged edge‑node targeting. In addition, they routinely launch mass spear‑phishing offensives with recipient lists extending into thousands of government staff members worldwide. Their campaign patterns reveal a mix of overt disruption (cloud outages) and covert infiltration (Duke families), suggesting an evolving capability to switch between high‑visibility and stealth operations as situational imperatives dictate. The actor’s historic linkage to notable APT campaigns—particularly those attributed to Cozy Bear/APT29—and the reuse of similar tool families implies either shared resources or a potential rebranding strategy. Victim types span critical infrastructure, defense and diplomatic networks, with an underlying inclination toward cloud‑dependent services and enterprise portals.
description: ZeffSec, a hybrid hacktivist/APT group, targets critical government and infrastructure cloud services, delivering large‑scale DDoS campaigns to edge nodes and leveraging extensive spear‑phishing to obtain access before quick data exfiltration. Their most publicized operation was a massive March 2026 attack on Iran’s ArvanCloud, which generated 504 Gateway Timeouts across multiple platforms. The group’s tactics suggest an emphasis on disruption and, potentially, opportunistic intelligence gathering.
goals: ZeffSec appears to operate on a dual mandate: public disruption of critical cloud and edge infrastructures to further ideological or protest objectives, while also exploiting compromised systems for rapid information gathering or potential ransom. Their primary focus remains national defensive sectors—governmental, defense, intelligence, finance, energy and transport—but they have also targeted the broader media, education, healthcare and manufacturing supply chains across a global footprint that includes the United States, Iran, Russia and multiple European allies. The tactical shift between noisy “smash‑and‑grab” DDoS assaults and more measured clandestine persistence indicates an adaptable strategy that can be tailored to either overt damage or covert reconnaissance based on situational objectives.
